entries.name: Northern Arizona University
entries.attribution: Zach Dischner · City photo, not campus
entries.sourceTitle: File:Flagstaff Fire By Night (7853997822).jpg
entries.imageDescription:
Since I have a smattering of photos from around the country, and hemisphere, from this summer, its just gonna be a random mess of posts from now on. 
  This was taken from the University of Colorado campus parking garage during the Flagstaff Fire that happened last June. Luckily, this night we had to frantically drive through the night from Boulder, CO to Palestine, TX for some thermal vac testing on our fancy instrument I and my team-mates designed all year. So no smoke/lung damage! Only sleep deprevation and a few stress-induced anxiety attacks haha!
 
Also, note the ugly lights on the left half of the screen. Colors rarely transfer well, but I call these the UTI lights. The true color is exactly what I think that of a Urinary Tract Infection would look like.

entries.name: University of Arizona
entries.attribution: US Department of Agriculture, National Resources Conservation Service, Phoenix, Arizona · City photo, not campus
entries.sourceTitle: File:Soil Shrink Swell Map of Tucson Arizona.jpg
entries.imageDescription:
Clay in the soil causes it to shrink and swell, which may crack building foundations, concrete
  Soil Properties: Shrink/Swell Potential 
  A soil survey contains maps and a description of each major soil in the survey area. More important, the survey describes how soil properties affect a wide range of rural and urban land uses. One of these properties, shrink/swell potential, is of great importance in the construction industry.
  Shrink/swell potential is the relative change in volume to be expected with changes in moisture content, that is, the extent to which the soil shrinks as it dries out or swells when it gets wet. Extent of shrinking and swelling is influenced by the amount and kind of clay in the soil. Shrinking and swelling of soils causes much damage to building foundations, roads and other structures. A high shrink/swell potential indicates a hazard to maintenance of structures built in, on, or with material having this rating. Moderate and low ratings lessen the hazard accordingly. 
 
Source:  https://www.nrcs.usda.gov/wps/portal/nrcs/az/soils/surveys/nrcs144p2_065083/

Construction began in 1163 under Bishop Maurice de Sully and lasted until the 14th century. Built on the Île de la Cité, it became the religious and political center of France. Its characteristic features include the two 69-meter-high western towers, the large rose window, filigree tracery, and the famous gargoyles. The cathedral is approximately 130 meters long and impresses with its high, light-flooded nave. Throughout history, Notre Dame has been the scene of significant events, such as Napoleon’s coronation in 1804. In the 19th century, it was restored under the direction of Eugène Viollet-le-Duc, who also created the striking crossing tower. On April 15, 2019, a major fire destroyed large parts of the roof and the crossing tower. Since then, extensive reconstruction work has been underway. Notre Dame is considered a masterpiece of medieval architecture and a symbol of French history, culture, and identity.

entries.imageDescription: Cork figure at LVM insurance in  Münster ,  North Rhine-Westphalia , Germany  The origins of today’s LVM campus date back to 1967, when the company moved into its premises on Kolde-Ring at the corner of  Weseler  Straße. The campus’s seven insurance buildings are located south of Münster city center. The northern part of Von-Stauffenberg-Straße runs through the campus, while Sperlichstraße forms its southern boundary. The LVM buildings were constructed between 1965 and 2014. The insurance company’s three high-rise buildings in particular are part of Münster’s  skyline . The ground-level sculptures “Body and Soul” (Duk-Kyu Ryang, 2015) and “Two Horses for Münster” ( Stephan Huber , 2002) are central visual elements of the site design. The 63-meter-high office tower LVM 5, known as “Crystal”, is a particularly striking building due to its design, while the 80-meter-high building LVM 3, known as “Tower”, is one of the tallest buildings in Münster.

entries.name: Rochester Institute of Technology of Dubai
entries.attribution: Member of the  Expedition 22  crew. · City photo, not campus
entries.sourceTitle: File:Artificial Archipelagos, Dubai, United Arab Emirates ISS022-E-024940 lrg.jpg
entries.imageDescription:
The municipality of Dubai is the largest city of the Persian Gulf emirate of the same name, and has built a global reputation for large-scale developments and architectural works. Among the most visible of these developments—particularly from the perspective of astronauts on board the International Space Station—are three human-made archipelagos. The two Palm Islands (Palm Jumeirah and Palm Jebel Ali) appear as stylized palm trees when viewed from above. The World Islands evoke a rough map of the world from an air- or space-borne perspective. Palm Jumeirah and the World Islands are highlighted in this astronaut photograph.
 Palm Jumeirah (image lower left) was begun in 2001 and required more than 50 million cubic meters of dredged sand to raise the islands above the Persian Gulf sea level. Construction of the Palm Jumeirah islands was completed in 2006; the islands are now being developed for residential and commercial housing and infrastructure. Creation of the 300 World Islands (image upper right) was begun in 2003 and completed in 2008, using 320 million cubic meters of sand and 37 million tonnes of rock for the surrounding 27-kilometer-long protective breakwater. Little to no infrastructure development of The World is apparent in this astronaut photograph.
 
Also visible at the lower edge of the astronaut photograph is another notable structure—the Burj Khalifa (image lower right and rotated 90 degrees in inset). Burj Khalifa stands 800 meters (2,600 feet) high, and it is currently the world’s tallest structure. The astronaut photograph captures enough detail to make out the tapering outline of the building as well as its dark, needle-like shadow pointing towards the northeast.
